A couple of days ago a friend of mine had heart attack symptoms. He's in good shape, not fat, and in his 40s. We're both ex-pats living and working in a third-world country, and having an acute life-threatening medical emergency is pretty much the nightmare scenario for western ex-pats. He had a mutual friend take him to the hospital (military hospital, so not as bad as it could have been). Like I said, he's in good shape, and they started running tests. Not a heart attack... even worse: an aortic aneurysm. That's the sort of thing that will kill you in short order.

Long story short, he was under the knife for most of the night but he made it. The doctor said it probably should have killed him, and would have killed him if he had delayed coming in very long, but the fact that he's in such good shape saved his life. If he'd been fat (like a lot of my fellow ex-pats are), he probably wouldn't have survived.

Anyone can have a medical emergency, and it's possible to do everything right and still die from something like that, but fatties are 1) more likely to have life-threatening episodes at much young ages, and 2) more likely to die when they happen. We'll see if that's enough of a wake-up call to get some of these guys off the couch. I'm not holding my breath.

Edit: I should specify that he had some sort of congenital contributing factor (I don't know all the details - just that it wasn't as much of a surprise as it would have been otherwise). He's doing well under the circumstances, although the road to recovery looks to be a long one. He was doing things right as far as weight, exercise, and diet. It was "just one of those things"... the point is that "those things" are a lot more likely to happen to fat people - and kill them when they do happen - than fit people like him.

Risk factors for aortic aneurysms:

  • Coronary artery disease
  • Hypertension
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Hyperhomocysteinemia
  • Elevated C-reactive protein
  • Tobacco use
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Marfan syndrome
  • Ehlers-Danlos type IV
  • Bicuspid Aortic Valve
  • Syphilis
  • IgG4-related disease
